Hairy Da Ding Herb (Mao Da Ding Cao)
Source: https://zhongyibaike.com/wiki/%E6%AF%9B%E5%A4%A7%E4%B8%81%E8%8D%89
Name
Small One-Branch Arrow (Xiao Yi Zhi Jian), One-Branch Fragrance (Yi Zhi Xiang), Rabbit-Ear Wind (Tu Er Feng), Hairy-Ear Wind (Mao Er Feng), Windless Self-Moving Herb (Wu Feng Zi Dong Cao), Ground-Adherent Wind (Tie Di Feng), One Incense Stick (Yi Zhu Xiang), White Eyebrow (Bai Mei), One Branch Herb on the Crown (Tou Ding Yi Zhi Cao), Ground-Adherent Disperser (Tie Di Xiao), Badi Fragrance (Ba Di Xiang), Four-Skin Fragrance (Si Pi Xiang), Full-Ground Fragrance (Man Di Xiang), Prostrate Old (Fu Di Lao), Sky Lantern Core (Tian Deng Xin), Ground-Locking Tiger (Suo Di Hu), White-Flower Single-Branch Incense (Bai Hua Yi Zhi Xiang), One Branch Herb on the Crown (Tou Ding Yi Zhi Cao), Ground-Pouncing Fragrance (Pu Di Xiang), Grinding-Ground Fragrance (Mo Di Xiang), Silver Tall Cup (Yin Gao Bei), Hairy Fu Lang Flower (Mao Fu Lang Hua)
Small One-Branch Arrow (Xiao Yi Zhi Jian)
Rabbit-Ear Wind (Tu Er Feng)
Cultivation and Preparation of Mao Da Ding Cao (Mao Da Ding Cao)
Source
The whole herb of the Asteraceae plant Mao Da Ding Cao (Mao Da Ding Cao). Harvest in summer, wash clean, sun-dry or use fresh.
[Morphology]
Mao Da Ding Cao (Mao Da Ding Cao) is a perennial herb. Rhizomes short and stout, densely covered with white cottony hairs; numerous fibrous roots, dark brown. Leaves basal; with short petioles; leaf blades soft and thick, oblong or obovate, 5–10 cm long, 2.5–4.5 cm wide, apex blunt-rounded, base cuneate, margins entire, young leaves with soft hairs on the upper surface that fall off with age, underside densely covered with white cottony hairs. Flower stems erect, solitary, 10–40 cm high, covered with light brown cottony hairs; capitulum solitary at stem apex, about 3.5 cm in diameter; involucre in two series, linear-lanceolate, outer series slightly shorter, back densely covered with light brown cottony hairs; ligulate florets white, female, bilabiate, outer lip elongated with three lobes, inner series small with two deep lobes; tubular florets bisexual, corolla slightly bilabiate. Achenes linear-lanceolate, about 5 mm long, slightly flattened, with longitudinal ribs and fine hairs, beak very short at flowering and equal to the achene at maturity; pappus about 1 cm long, pale red, glossy. Flowering period May–June.
[Habitat and Distribution]
Ecological environment: grows on sunny slopes, grasslands and forest edges.
Resource distribution: distributed in Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian, Hunan, Guangdong, Guangxi, Sichuan, Guizhou, Yunnan and Tibet.
Properties and Flavor
Bitter and pungent, neutral in nature.
1. "Tianbao Materia Medica": pungent, warm.
2. "Guangxi Record of Chinese Materia Medica": taste bitter, slightly sweet and pungent, neutral in nature, non-toxic.
Characteristics
Rhizomes clustered with many fibrous roots, roots may reach up to 11 cm, surface brownish; brittle texture, fracture yellow-white. Leaves clustered, often wrinkled; intact leaves when flattened are oblong or ovate, upper surface dark brown, underside brownish, covered with yellow-white downy hairs; brittle texture, some leaves contain a brown-yellow flower, peduncles hollow. Slight odor, astringent taste.
Prefer specimens with many leaves and little fragmentation.
Effects of Mao Da Ding Cao (Mao Da Ding Cao)
Efficacy
The whole herb of the Asteraceae plant Mao Da Ding Cao (Mao Da Ding Cao). Used for common cold with cough, epigastric distension and pain, diarrhea, dysentery, edema, turbid urinary discharge, sores and carbuncles, traumatic swelling and pain, and poisonous snake bites.
Meridians/Channels
1. "Sichuan Record of Chinese Materia Medica": enters the Liver and Lung meridians.
2. "Mindong Materia Medica": enters the Spleen, Kidney and Bladder meridians.
Indications
Clears heat and detoxifies, disseminates the Lung and stops cough, moves qi and activates blood. Indicated for common cold cough, epigastric distension and pain, diarrhea, dysentery, edema, turbid urinary discharge, sores and carbuncles, traumatic swelling and pain, and poisonous snake bites.
1. "Illustrated Examination of Plant Names and Realities": treats pediatric food accumulation (infant indigestion).
2. "Classification of Herbal Properties": disperses cold, treats cough and rheumatism.
3. "Tianbao Materia Medica": treats boils and ulcerations, and eruptive sores on the back.
4. "Compilation of Commonly Used Folk Herbs": promotes Lung qi, induces sweating, disperses cold and dispels wind, stops cough and calms wheezing, stops pertussis.
5. "Jiangxi Folk Herbs": treats unilateral headache and toothache; for children with high fever, irritability and thirst, and acute convulsions, decoct and take orally. Crush and apply to local sores and carbuncles.
6. "Sichuan Record of Chinese Materia Medica": treats leucorrhea due to yin deficiency, nocturnal emission and spermatorrhea, facial edema. Also applied externally for ulcerated bone with phlegm discharge.
7. "Mindong Materia Medica": expels dampness, moves qi, promotes urination, unblocks menses and breaks blood stasis. Treats edema, distention, hernia, prolapse, jaundiced obesity, amenorrhea, food accumulation, soreness of the waist and hips, and urinary retention.
Usage and Dosage
Internal use: decoction, 6–15 g dried, 30–60 g fresh.
External use: appropriate amount, crush and apply as a poultice.
Formulas using Mao Da Ding Cao (Mao Da Ding Cao)
1. For common cold with cough: Rabbit-Ear Wind (Tu Er Feng) 2 qian,
Tiger-Ear Herb (Hu Er Cao)
2 qian. Decoction, take once.
2. For cough and asthma: Rabbit-Ear Wind (Tu Er Feng) 1 liang, steam with honey and eat.
3. For pulmonary abscess: Rabbit-Ear Wind (Tu Er Feng) 2 liang. Decoction with equal parts water and wine. (Formula from "Guiyang Folk Herbs")
4. For edema: Mao Da Ding Cao (Mao Da Ding Cao), Pi Di Gua (Pi Di Gua), and brown sugar each 1 liang, wine 4 liang. Boil the two medicinal herbs in two bowls of water until reduced to one bowl, then add sugar and wine and simmer to take. One dose daily for three consecutive days.
5. For urethritis with bloody urination: fresh Mao Da Ding Cao (Mao Da Ding Cao) 1 liang. Wash and decoct, add rock sugar, take twice daily.
6. For dysentery: fresh Mao Da Ding Cao (Mao Da Ding Cao) 2 liang (dried 1 liang), decoct two bowls of water down to 0.8 bowl, sweeten with
honey
take internally before meals, three consecutive doses. (Formulas from "Mindong Materia Medica")
7. For qi stagnation causing epigastric pain: Mao Da Ding Cao (Mao Da Ding Cao) 5 qian to 1 liang. Decoction or simmer with wine and take.
8. For wind-cold diarrhea: Mao Da Ding Cao (Mao Da Ding Cao) 5 qian to 1 liang. Decoction and take.
9. For rheumatic edema: fresh Mao Da Ding Cao (Mao Da Ding Cao) 1 to 2 liang. Decoction and take. (Formulas from "Fujian Chinese Herbs")
10. For pediatric malnutrition (gān jī): Mao Da Ding Cao (Mao Da Ding Cao) 3 qian, together with
chicken liver
one or
pork liver
2 liang, add water and decoct, remove the herbs, eat the liver and soup. (From "Jiangxi Folk Herbs")
11. For traumatic injuries and bruises: Mao Da Ding Cao (Mao Da Ding Cao) 5 qian to 1 liang. Decoction, mix with sweet wine and take. (From "Mindong Materia Medica")

Cultivation and Processing of Calcite (Han Shui Shi)
Source
It is the crystal of the sulfate mineral mirabilite (Mang Xiao).
Taste and Properties
Pungent and salty; cold in nature.
Appearance
Usually occurs as regular massive crystals, often in a rhombic-prismatic form, with edges and angles; colorless or yellowish-white, transparent, slightly translucent or opaque, surface smooth with a glassy luster. Hard in texture, easily broken; fragments are square or rectangular. Odorless, with a mild taste.
Effects of Calcite (Han Shui Shi)
Functions
It is the crystal of the sulfate mineral mirabilite (Mang Xiao).
Main indications: febrile epidemic diseases, accumulated heat with vexation and thirst, vomiting and diarrhea, edema, urinary retention, gum bleeding, erysipelas, and burns.
Channels
Enters
Heart meridian (Xin Jing)
,
Stomach meridian (Wei Jing)
, Kidney meridian (Shen Jing)
.
Indications
Clears heat and reduces fire, opens the orifices, reduces swelling. Treats febrile epidemic diseases, accumulated heat with vexation and thirst, vomiting and diarrhea, edema, urinary retention, gum bleeding, erysipelas, and burns.
① Ben Jing: Indicated for body heat, accumulation of pathogenic qi in the abdomen, skin burning like fire, vexation and fullness, and water accumulation.
② Ben Cao Jing Ji Zhu: Counteracts croton (Ba Dou) poisoning.
③ Bie Lu: Removes epidemic heat, latent heat in the five viscera, stomach heat, vexation and fullness, thirst, edema, and lower abdominal obstruction.
④ Yi Xue Ru Men: Treats pediatric erysipelas; burn to powder, mix with vinegar and apply topically.
⑤ Gang Mu: Treats whitish urine, internal obstruction, cools the blood and reduces fire, stops toothache, strengthens the teeth and clears the eyes.
⑥ Yi Lin Zuan Yao: Eliminates delirious heat; treats great epidemic heat and cholera-like vomiting and diarrhea, vexation and thirst, and damp-heat edema.
⑦ Ben Cao Qiu Zhen: Applied topically for scalds and burns.
⑧ Ben Cao Qiu Yuan: Treats true heat in the heart and kidney.
Dosage and Administration
Internal use: decocted as a decoction, 9–15 g; or used in pills or powders.
External use: grind to a powder and mix or apply as a paste topically.
Precautions and Contraindications
Contraindicated in patients with deficiency-cold of the spleen and stomach.
① Ben Cao Jing Ji Zhu: Avoid use with Di Shu.
② Ben Cao Jing Shu: Not suitable for those with yin deficiency and flourishing fire, coughing up blood, excessive phlegm, tidal fever and steaming bone disorder, or those with spleen and stomach leading to diarrhea.
③ Ben Cao Qiu Zhen: Absolutely contraindicated in deficient persons with floating heat.
Prescriptions using Calcite (Han Shui Shi)
① For accumulated heat in the zang-fu organs and epidemic heat causing vexation and thirst: Condensed Water Stone (Ning Shui Shi),
Gypsum (Shi Gao),
Talc (Hua Shi) each five qian, Licorice (Gan Cao) two qian. Grind to a powder. Each dose one qian, taken with plain water. (Fang Mai Zheng Zong)
② For typhoid with madness, or throwing off clothes and running about, climbing walls and roofs: Calcite (Han Shui Shi),
Coptis (Huang Lian) (pith removed) equal parts. Grind finely; each dose two qian, steep in a strong decoction of Licorice (Gan Cao), let cool and take. (Ben Shi Fang — Que Shi San)
③ To remove heat-induced epilepsy:
Rhubarb (Da Huang),
Dried Ginger (Gan Jiang),
Dragon Bone (Long Gu) four liang each,
Cinnamon Twig (Gui Zhi) three liang,
Licorice (Gan Cao),
Oyster Shell (Mu Li) two liang each,
Calcite (Han Shui Shi),
Talc (Hua Shi),
Halloysite (Chi Shi Zhi),
White Halloysite (Bai Shi Zhi),
Amethyst (Zi Shi Ying),
Gypsum (Shi Gao) six liang each. The above twelve ingredients are pounded and coarsely sifted, placed in a deerskin bag; take a three-finger pinch, boil in three sheng of well water to three boils, take one sheng warm. (Jin Kui Yao Lue — Feng Yin Tang)

Cultivation and Processing of Hibiscus syriacus Flower (Mùjǐn huā)
Source
This item is the dried flowers of the Malvaceae plant Hibiscus syriacus that are not fully open.
Processing
Hibiscus syriacus Flower: remove stems and other impurities from the crude drug and sieve off dust.
Honey-fried Hibiscus syriacus Flower: take Hibiscus flowers and fry according to the honey-frying method until the honey is fully absorbed. For every 100 kg of Hibiscus flowers, use 40 kg of refined honey.
Characters
1. Hibiscus syriacus Flower
The product is wrinkled, ovate or irregularly cylindrical, often with short flower stalks. The whole is pubescent, length 1.5–3.5 cm, width 1–2 cm. Bracts 6–7, linear. Calyx bell-shaped, gray-yellow-green, apex 5-lobed, lobes triangular. Petals are white, yellowish-white or light brownish-yellow; single petals number 5 or double petals exceed 10. Stamens are numerous, filaments united into a tube. Slight fragrance, bland taste.
2. Honey-fried Hibiscus syriacus Flower
Pale yellow-brown to yellow-brown, moist, has a honey aroma, slightly sweet in taste.
Properties and Meridian Tropism
Sweet, bland, cool. Enters the Spleen and Lung channels.
Functions and Indications
Clears heat and drains dampness, cools the blood and detoxifies. Indicated for intestinal-wind bloody diarrhea, dysentery with red or white stools, bleeding hemorrhoids, lung-heat cough, cough with blood, leukorrhea, sores and carbuncles, and burns.
Dosage and Administration
For internal use, decocted, 3–9 g.
For external use, an appropriate amount of fresh material, crushed and applied to the affected area.
Effects of Hibiscus syriacus Flower (Mùjǐn huā)
Efficacy
This item is the dried, not fully opened flowers of the Malvaceae plant Hibiscus syriacus. Used for intestinal-wind bloody diarrhea, dysentery with red or white stools, bleeding hemorrhoids, lung-heat cough, cough with blood, leukorrhea, sores and carbuncles, and burns.
Prescriptions Using Hibiscus syriacus Flower (Mùjǐn huā)
1. For dysenteric diarrhea with clenched mouth: remove the calyxes from red Hibiscus flowers, shade-dry and grind to powder; first boil two flatbread cakes, dip them in the powder and eat. (Jìjí Xiānfāng)
2. For dysentery with red or white stools: one liang of Hibiscus flowers (half for children), decoct in water, mix with three fen of white honey and take. Use red flowers for bloody dysentery, white flowers for white dysentery; avoid sour and cold foods. (Yúnnán Zhōngyī Yànfāng)
3. For vomiting blood, lower-body bleeding, and dysentery with red or white stools: 9 to 13 Hibiscus flowers. Add boiling water and rock sugar as appropriate, steep for half an hour, take before meals, twice daily. (Fújiàn Mínjiān Cǎoyào)
4. For wind-phlegm obstructing and causing reversal: sun-dry Hibiscus flowers, roast and grind; take one or two spoonfuls per dose, take with boiling water on an empty stomach; white flowers are especially good. (Jiǎnbiàn Dānfāng)
5. For nausea and gastric reversal: thousand-petalled white Hibiscus flowers, shade-dry and powder; mix with aged rice soup and give three to five sips; if there is no change, then adjust and take rice gruel. (Xiùzhēn Fāng — Jǐnhuā sǎn)
6. For female leukorrhea: two qian of Hibiscus flowers, powdered, mixed with human breast milk, spread on rice and steam until cooked, then eat. (Diānnán Běncǎo)
7. For treatment of sores and carbuncles: appropriate amount of fresh Hibiscus flowers, a little sweet rice wine, mash and apply externally. (Jiāngxī Cǎoyào)

Honeysuckle Flower, Japanese Honeysuckle
Honeysuckle Flower (Ren Dong Hua), Egret Flower (Lu Si Hua), Silver Flower (Yin Hua), Double Flower (Shuang Hua), Two-Flower (Er Hua), Golden Vine Flower (Jin Teng Hua), Double Bract Flower (Shuang Bao Hua), Golden Flower (Jin Hua), Two-Treasure Flower (Er Bao Hua)

Cultivation and Processing of Honeysuckle Flower (Jin Yin Hua)
Source
The flower buds of plants of the Caprifoliaceae family, Lonicera species. Pick the buds in May to June on clear mornings just after the dew has dried; spread on mats to sun-dry or dry in the shade, turning frequently to prevent blackening. Avoid exposure to strong sunlight. Store in a dry, well-ventilated place to prevent insect infestation and discoloration.
[Habitat and Distribution]
Produced in most regions of China, with Shandong having the largest output and Henan producing the better quality.
Properties and Taste
Sweet; cold
Characteristics
Dried flower buds are long, rod-like, slightly curved, about 2–3 centimeters long, thicker at the upper end, about 1.5–3 millimeters in diameter. The exterior is yellow or yellow-brown, covered with short soft hairs and glandular hairs. At the base are small green calyces, 5-lobed; the lobes are triangular and hairless. When the bud is split open, five stamens and one pistil are visible. The corolla is bilabiate; the stamens and pistil extend like beards. Aromatic odor, slightly bitter taste. Best when the flowers are unopened, yellow-white, and plump.
Effects of Honeysuckle Flower (Jin Yin Hua)
Efficacy
The flower buds of Lonicera species of the Caprifoliaceae family.
Main indications: febrile disease fever, dysentery due to heat-toxin, carbuncles and boils, swellings and toxins, scrofula, hemorrhoids and anal fistula.
Meridians
Lung Meridian; Stomach Meridian
Indications
Clears heat and relieves toxicity. Treats fever in febrile diseases, dysentery due to heat-toxin, carbuncles and boils, swellings and toxins, scrofula, hemorrhoids and anal fistula.
① Dian Nan Ben Cao: clears heat, treats various sores, carbuncles and back eruptions, vaginal discharge, and scrofula.
② Sheng Cao Yao Xing Bei Yao: can disperse carbuncles and sores, stop dysenteric diarrhea, wash criptic sores, and remove heat in the skin and blood.
③ Ben Cao Bei Yao: nourishes blood and stops thirst. Treats scabies and tinea.
④ Chongqing Tang Miscellaneous Notes: clears collaterals from wind-fire-damp-heat, resolves febrile epidemics and foul turbidity, calms liver and gallbladder rising wind yang, treats convulsions and epilepsy.
⑤ Guangzhou Military Common Chinese Herbs Manual: clears heat and detoxifies. Treats external contraction fever and cough, enteritis, bacillary dysentery, measles, mumps, septicemia, sores and boils, appendicitis, wound infections, and infantile prickly toxin. Prepared as a cold herbal tea, it can prevent heatstroke, colds, and intestinal infectious diseases.
Dosage and Administration
Internal use: decoct as a tea, 10–20 g; or used in pills or powders.
External use: appropriate amount, crushed and applied as a poultice.
Precautions and Contraindications
Contraindicated for spleen and stomach deficiency cold and for ulcers or sores with clear pus due to qi deficiency.
Prescriptions Using Honeysuckle Flower (Jin Yin Hua)
① Prevention of Japanese encephalitis and meningococcal meningitis: Honeysuckle Flower (Jin Yin Hua), Forsythia (Lian Qiao), Isatis Root (Da Qing Gen), Reed Root (Lu Gen), Licorice Root (Gan Cao) each 3 qian. Decoction as a tea, one dose daily, take continuously for three to five days. (Jiangxi Herbal Medicine)
② Treat Taiyin wind-warmth, warm-heat at onset in winter-warm disease where fever is present without aversion to cold but with thirst: Forsythia (Lian Qiao) 1 liang, Honeysuckle Flower (Jin Yin Hua) 1 liang, Bitter Platycodon Root (Ku Jie Geng) 6 qian, Mint (Bo He) 6 qian, Bamboo Leaves (Dan Zhu Ye) 4 qian, Raw Licorice (Sheng Gan Cao) 5 qian, Schizonepeta Spike (Jing Jie Sui) 4 qian, Fermented Soybean (Dan Dou Chi) 5 qian, Burdock Fruit (Niu Bang Zi) 6 qian. Grind to powder; take 6 qian per dose, decoct in fresh reed root soup for drinking. (Wen Bing Tiao Bian — Yin Qiao San)
③ Treat dysentery: Honeysuckle Flower (Jin Yin Hua) (dry roasted in a copper pot to preserve properties) 5 qian. For bloody ("red") dysentery, take with white honey water; for watery ("white") dysentery, take with rock sugar water. (Hui Zhi Tang Empirical Formula — Ren Dong San)
④ Treat hot strangury: Honeysuckle Flower (Jin Yin Hua), Sea Golden Sand Vine (Hai Jin Sha Teng), Tianhu Sui (Tian Hu Sui), Jin Xie Zi Root (Jin Xie Zi Gen), White Cogongrass Root (Bai Mao Gen) each 1 liang. Decoction, one dose daily, five to seven days per course. (Jiangxi Herbal Medicine)
⑤ Treat biliary tract infection and wound infection: Honeysuckle Flower (Jin Yin Hua) 1 liang, Forsythia (Lian Qiao), Isatis Root (Da Qing Gen), Scutellaria (Huang Qin), Wild Chrysanthemum Flower (Ye Ju Hua) each 5 qian. Decoction, one dose daily. (Jiangxi Herbal Medicine)
⑥ For severely painful sores with dark purple discoloration: Honeysuckle Flower with connected twigs and leaves (chopped) 2 liang, Astragalus Root (Huang Qi) 4 liang, Licorice Root (Gan Cao) 1 liang. Finely slice, add 1 liter of wine, place in a closed jar and boil in a heavy steam bath for two to three hours; remove, strain, and take immediately. (Huo Fa Ji Yao — Hui Chuang Jin Yin Hua San)
⑦ Treat all types of swellings and toxins, whether ulcerated or not, early-stage fever, and pus-forming boils, throat swelling, and lacteal issues: fresh juice of Honeysuckle Flower including stems and leaves half a bowl, decoct to four-fifths and take; use the residue topically to promote pus discharge, disperse toxin, regulate qi and blood — especially effective. (Ji Shan Tang Empirical Formulas)
⑧ Treat early-stage carbuncle on the back: Honeysuckle Flower 1/2 jin, boil 10 bowls of water down to 2 bowls, add Angelica Sinensis (Dang Gui) 2 liang, boil down to 1 bowl, take in one gulp. (Dong Tian Ao Zhi — Gui Hua Tang)
⑨ Treat all internal and external abscesses and swellings: Honeysuckle Flower 4 liang, Licorice Root (Gan Cao) 3 liang. Decoction, take immediately; those who can drink alcohol may decoct in wine. (Yi Xue Xin Wu — Ren Dong Tang)
⑩ Treat large intestinal abscess, with inability to press the hand, right leg flexed and unable to extend: Honeysuckle Flower 3 liang, Angelica Sinensis (Dang Gui) 2 liang, Sanguisorba (Di Yu) 1 liang, Ophiopogon Root (Mai Dong) 1 liang, Scrophularia Root (Xuan Shen) 1 liang, Raw Licorice (Sheng Gan Cao) 3 qian, Coix Seed (Yi Yi Ren) 5 qian, Scutellaria (Huang Qin) 2 qian. Decoction and drink. (Dong Tian Ao Zhi — Qing Chang Yin)
⑾ Treat deep-seated abscesses: Honeysuckle Flower, Wild Chrysanthemum (Ye Ju Hua), Sea Golden Sand (Hai Jin Sha), Malan (Ma Lan), Licorice Root (Gan Cao) each 3 qian, Isatis Leaf (Da Qing Ye) 1 liang. Decoction. Also used for treating carbuncles and boils. (Jiangxi Herbal Medicine)
⑿ Treat gaseous gangrene and osteomyelitis: Honeysuckle Flower 1 liang, Centella asiatica (Ji Xue Cao) 2 liang, Yi Dian Hong 1 liang, Wild Chrysanthemum Flower (Ye Ju Hua) 1 liang, White Cogongrass Root (Bai Mao Gen) 1 liang, Oldenlandia diffusa (Bai Hua She She Cao) 2 liang, Di Dan Cao 1 liang. Decoction. Externally also apply mashed fresh Ligustrum Fruit (Nu Zhen Zi) and Fo Jia Cao appropriately. (Jiangxi Herbal Medicine)
⒀Treat early acute mastitis: Honeysuckle Flower 8 qian, Dandelion (Pu Gong Ying) 5 qian, Forsythia (Lian Qiao) and Aged Tangerine Peel (Chen Pi) each 3 qian, Green Tangerine Peel (Qing Pi) and Raw Licorice (Sheng Gan Cao) each 2 qian. Prepare one dose, decoct twice and divide into two doses per day; for severe cases, take two doses per day. (Zhong Ji Yi Kan, 1964)
⒁Treat chronic mammary lumps that gradually enlarge, red and exuding fluid, with deep internal ulceration: Honeysuckle Flower and raw Astragalus Root each 5 qian, Angelica Sinensis (Dang Gui) 8 qian, Licorice Root (Gan Cao) 1 qian 8 fen, Citrus Leaves (Guo Ju Ye, i.e., Chou Ju Ye) 50 leaves. Decoction in half water and half wine. (Zhu Lin Nu Ke — Yin Hua Tang)
⒂Treat Yangmei-related toxins: Honeysuckle Flower 1 liang, Licorice Root (Gan Cao) 2 qian, Wild Black Beans (Hei Liao Dou / Ye Liao Dou) 2 liang, Smilax Glabra (Tu Fu Ling) 4 liang. Decoction, one dose daily, drink all. (Wai Ke Shi Fa — Ren Dong Tang)
⒃Antidote for organophosphate pesticide poisoning (e.g., 1059, 1605, 4049): Honeysuckle Flower 2–3 liang, Alum (Ming Fan) 2 qian, Rhubarb (Da Huang) 5 qian, Licorice Root (Gan Cao) 2–3 liang. Decoction and drink cold; take one prepared dose at a time, twice daily. (Xuzhou Compilation of Single-formula and Proven Remedies)
⒄Treat sores and back carbuncles, promote suppuration, relieve pain and drain pus: Honeysuckle Flower 4 liang, Licorice Root (Gan Cao) 1 liang (stir-fried). Grind coarsely; take 4 qian per dose, decoct in one cup water and one cup wine down to one cup, strain and take while warm. (Wei Sheng Bao Jian)
⒅After recovery from diabetes to prevent the occurrence of carbuncles and boils, take: the whole honeysuckle plant (roots, stems, flowers, and leaves) in any amount, place in a jar, soak in good grain alcohol, roast overnight over chaff fire, remove and sun-dry. Add a little licorice, grind into fine powder, make paste with the soaking alcohol and form into pills the size of a Chinese scholar-bean. Take 50–100 pills per dose with water or wine as desired. This medicine not only treats carbuncles but is especially good at stopping thirst. (Ben Cao Gang Mu citing Wai Ke Jing Yao)
[Dietary Therapy Recipes]
1. Honeysuckle and Mung Bean Drink
Mung beans 60 g, boil to extract juice; add Honeysuckle Flower (Jin Yin Hua) 10 g and appropriate honey. Simmer 20–30 minutes, strain and drink.
Function: clears heat, relieves vexation, relieves summer heat and thirst. Indications: summer-heat vexation and thirst, short and reddish urination, or prickly heat and itching. Also used to help prevent heatstroke.
2. Chrysanthemum, Honeysuckle and Dandelion Tea
Chrysanthemum Flower (Ju Hua) 15 g, Honeysuckle Flower (Jin Yin Hua) 20 g, Dandelion (Pu Gong Ying) 30 g, Licorice Root (Gan Cao) 3 g, Mung Beans 20 g. Put all ingredients into a pot, decoct and strain to obtain the liquid. One dose daily, use continuously for 5–7 days as one course.
Function: clears heat and detoxifies, anti-infective. Indication: early-stage mastitis in women with significant heat-toxin.
3. Two-Flower Tea
Honeysuckle Flower (Jin Yin Hua) 50 g, Hang Chrysanthemum (Hang Ju Hua) 100 g, honey to taste. Pick out impurities from the honeysuckle and chrysanthemum, rinse and lightly fry in a pot, cool and store in a clean jar. When needed, take a small amount, place in a cup, pour boiling water and steep, sweeten with honey as desired. Take 2–3 times daily.
Function: clears heat and dispels wind, brightens the eyes and lowers blood pressure. Indications: summer heat vexation and thirst, hypertension, coronary heart disease, palpitations and insomnia, sore throat, cold and cough. Also suitable as a cooling summer beverage.
4. Ren Dong Decoction (Honeysuckle Decoction)
Honeysuckle Flower (Jin Yin Hua) 120 g, Licorice Root (Gan Cao) 45 g. Decoct in water or wine and take as a tea. Indication: treats "all internal and external swellings and abscesses," such as intestinal abscesses, mastitis, and boils.

Source: https://zhongyibaike.com/wiki/%E6%9C%A8%E8%B4%BC
Name
Common Scouring Rush Herb, Herb of Common Scouring Rush, Herb of Dutch Rushes, Herb of Rough Horsetail, Herb of Scouring Rush
Scouring Rush Herb (Mu Zei Cao), File Herb (Cuo Cao), Jointed-stem Herb (Jie Jie Cao), Knotted-bone Herb (Jie Gu Cao), Rattle Herb (Xiang Cao), Bone-joining Leaf (Jie Gu Ye), Pen-stem Herb (Bi Gan Cao), Pen-tube Herb (Bi Tong Cao), Scouring Herb (Ca Cao), Heartless Herb (Wu Xin Cao), Pen-tip Herb (Bi Tou Cao), Pen-tube Herb (Bi Guan Cao)
Cuo Cao (File Herb)
Wu Xin Cao (Heartless Herb)
Mu Zei Cao (Scouring Rush Herb)
Jie Jie Cao (Jointed-stem Herb)

Cultivation and Processing of Common Scouring Rush (Mu Zei)
Source
This item is the dried aerial part of the Equisetaceae plant Common Scouring Rush (Mu Zei), Equisetum hiemale L. Harvest in summer and autumn, remove impurities, sun-dry or shade-dry.
Nature and Flavor
Sweet, bitter; neutral.
Preparation
Remove withered stems and remaining roots, spray with clean water, moisten slightly, cut into sections, dry.
Characteristics
The dried whole herb is long and tube-shaped, hollow with nodes, unbranched. Length 30–60 centimeters, diameter about 5 millimeters, each internode 3–6 centimeters long. Surface gray-green or yellow-green, with numerous longitudinal branches arranged straight, densely bearing fine spines, producing a rough feel to the touch. At the nodes there are tubular dark-brown scale leaves that are easily detached at the nodes. Texture brittle, easily broken; fracture surface hollow, inside with gray-white or light-green thin pith. Odor none; taste sweet, slightly bitter and astringent. The best quality has stems that are thick and long, green in color, firm in texture, and not easily shed at the nodes.
Effects of Common Scouring Rush (Mu Zei)
Efficacy
This item is the dried aerial part of the Equisetaceae plant Common Scouring Rush (Mu Zei).
Main Indications: cloudy films over the eyes, tearing in wind, intestinal wind with bleeding, bloody dysentery, malaria, sore throat, abscesses and swellings.
Channels
Enters
Lung channel, Liver channel.
Main Indications
Disperse wind and clear heat, release the muscle layer, dispel ocular films. Treats cloudy films over the eyes, tearing in wind, intestinal wind with bleeding, bloody dysentery, malaria, sore throat, and abscesses and swellings.
1. Jiahu Materia Medica (Jiahu Bencao): Indicated for eye diseases, expels ocular membranes. Also reduces accumulations and masses, benefits the liver and gallbladder, brightens the eyes, treats intestinal wind, stops dysentery and continuous uterine bleeding.
2. Compendium of Materia Medica (Bencao Gangmu): Releases the muscles, stops tearing, stops bleeding, expels wind-damp, relieves hernia pain, and treats prolapse of the large intestine.
3. Standard Materia Medica (Bencao Zheng): Induces sweating, releases the muscles. Treats typhoid and malaria. Expels wind-damp and disperses pathogenic fire.
4. Yuqiu’s Explanation of Medicines (Yu Qiu Yao Jie): Pacifies hard ulcerated swellings, expels wind and violent phlegm and saliva. Treats abscesses, scrofula, carbuncles, boils, tinea versicolor, scurf, and various uterine bleeding disorders, both red and white.
Dosage and Administration
Internal use: decoct 3–9 g, or include in pills or powders; external use: grind to powder and sprinkle.
Precautions and Contraindications
Use with caution in those with qi and blood deficiency.
1. Commentary on the Materia Medica (Bencao Jingshu): Eye diseases caused by anger and summer heat injuring the blood with violent redness, swelling and pain are not suitable for this herb.
2. Collected Sayings on Materia Medica (Bencao Huiyan): Excessive use harms the liver; not suitable for prolonged use.
3. Origins of This Classic (Benjing Fengyuan): Excessive use causes eye swelling; not suitable for long-standing ocular films or blood deficiency.
Formulas Using Common Scouring Rush (Mu Zei)
1. For eye obstruction with blurred vision and excessive tearing: Scouring Rush Herb (nodes removed) one liang, grind to powder, mix with sheep liver and pound into pills; take two qian each time morning and evening after meals, taken with plain soup. (Fangmai Zhengzong)
2. Blurry vision with excessive tearing: Scouring Rush (nodes removed) and Atractylodes Rhizome (Cang Zhu) (soaked in rice-washing water) one liang each, grind together to powder. Each dose two qian, take with tea. Or mix with honey to make pills and swallow. (Shenghui Fang)
3. For wind-cold-damp seeking to induce sweating: Scouring Rush (nodes removed) one liang, Fresh Ginger (Sheng Jiang) and White Part of Green Onion (Cong Bai) five qian each. Decoction in water, drink hot to induce sweating. (Shenghui Fang)
4. For intestinal wind with bleeding: Scouring Rush (nodes removed, fried) one liang, Mu Man (Mu Mantou) (fried), Bitter Orange (Zhi Ke, prepared), Sophora Fruit (Huai Jiao, fried), Poria (Fu Ling), Schizonepeta (Jing Jie) five qian each. Grind to powder; each dose two qian, take with a strongly decocted jujube (date) broth. (Renzhai Zhizhi Fang — Mu Zei Powder)
5. For persistent bloody dysentery: Scouring Rush five qian, decoct in water and take warm. One dose daily. (Shenghui Fang)
6. For chronic rectal prolapse not cured for years: Scouring Rush, amount not specified, char by burning (calcine) until persistence is achieved, grind to powder, apply to the anus and press. (Sanyin Fang)
7. For continuous menstrual bleeding: Scouring Rush (fried) three qian, water one cup decocted down to seven-tenths, take warm. One dose daily. (Shenghui Fang)
8. For external traumatic bleeding, gastrointestinal bleeding, gynecological bleeding and other hemorrhages: Scouring Rush 50%, Phellodendron Bark (Huang Bai) 20%, Motherwort (Yi Mu Cao) 20%, Chinese Gall (Wu Bei Zi) 10%. Grind each to powder, pass through a 120-mesh sieve, mix evenly. External: sprinkle powder on the wound and press with gauze. Internal: 2 g each time, every 4–6 hours. (Inner Mongolia Compilation of New Medical Methods of Chinese Herbal Medicine)
9. For restless fetus or threatened miscarriage: Scouring Rush (nodes removed) and Sichuan Lovage (Chuan Xiong) equal parts, grind to powder. Each dose three qian, decoct in one cup of water with Honeysuckle (Jin Yin Hua) one qian and take. (Shengji Zong Lu)
10. For red painful throat: crush fresh Scouring Rush and squeeze out the juice, mix with honey and take. (Quanzhou Materia Medica)
11. For edematous beriberi, nephritis with skin disease, edema: Scouring Rush 4 qian 5 fen, Duckweed (Fu Ping) three qian, Adzuki Bean (Chi Xiao Dou) three liang, Red Dates six pieces. Decoction in water, take three times daily. (Modern Practical Chinese Medicine)
12. For stiff tongue with bleeding: decoct Scouring Rush in water and gargle. (Shenghui Fang)
13. Acute throat obstruction: char Scouring Rush over a cow-dung fire (calcine), each dose one qian, take with cold water; when bleeding occurs the condition is relieved.
14. Unstoppable hemorrhage: same prescription as above, take twice daily.
15. Bleeding from internal hemorrhoids: Scouring Rush and Bitter Orange (Zhi Ke) each two liang, Dry Ginger (Gan Jiang) one liang, Rhubarb (Da Huang) two qian and a half; stir-fry together in a pan until blackened and charred (retaining efficacy), grind fine. Each dose two qian, take with millet soup. Very effective.
16. Female uterine hemorrhage: Scouring Rush and Cyperus Rhizome (Xiang Fu Zi) each one liang, Poxiao (Poxiao, niter) half a liang, grind to powder. Each dose three qian; if the blood is dark, decoct in one bowl of wine; if the blood is bright red, decoct in one bowl of water, take with the dregs. Take twice daily. If there is pain below the navel, add Frankincense (Ru Xiang), Myrrh (Mo Yao), and Angelica Sinensis (Dang Gui) one qian each and decoct together. Avoid raw, cold, hard foods and pork, fish, wheat products, etc. This formula is called Lei’s Mu Zei Powder.
17. Small intestine hernia: finely scrape Scouring Rush, lightly stir-fry to powder. Take two qian with boiling soup; effective. Can also be taken with hot wine.

Cultivation and Processing of Small Centipeda Herb (E bu shi cao)
Source
The whole herb of the Asteraceae plant Centipeda (Shi hu sui).
Taste and Properties
Taste: pungent; Nature: warm
Appearance
The whole herb is twisted together into clusters. Fibrous roots are thin, pale yellow; stems thin, much branched, brittle and easily broken, fracture surface yellowish-white. Leaves small, nearly sessile; leaf blades often wrinkled or fragmented, intact leaves when spread are spatulate, surface gray-green or brownish, margins with 3–5 teeth. Capitula (flower heads) yellow or yellow-brown. Odor slight, prolonged smelling causes an irritating sensation; taste bitter; slightly pungent.
Those with gray-green color and a strong pungent odor are best.
Effects of Small Centipeda Herb (E bu shi cao)
Functions
The whole herb of the Asteraceae plant Centipeda (Shi hu sui).
Treats common cold, cold-induced asthma, throat obstruction, whooping cough, sha-syndrome abdominal pain, amoebic dysentery, malaria, malnutrition-related diarrhea, rhinitis, nasal polyps, eye films causing gritty itching, scabies and tinea, traumatic injuries from falls and blows.
Meridians entered
Enters
Lung meridian
; Liver meridian
Main indications
Disperses wind and dispels cold, overcomes dampness and removes eye films, unblocks nasal obstruction. Treats common cold, cold-induced asthma, throat obstruction, whooping cough, sha-syndrome abdominal pain, amoebic dysentery, malaria, malnutrition-related diarrhea, rhinitis, nasal polyps, eye films causing gritty itching, scabies and tinea, traumatic injuries from falls and blows.
① "Supplement to Materia Medica" (Ben Cao Shi Yi): removes eye films; when pressed and stuffed into the nose, the film falls off by itself.
② "Si Sheng Materia Medica" (Four-Tone Materia Medica): unblocks nasal qi, benefits the nine orifices, expels wind-phlegm.
③ "Compendium of Materia Medica" (Ben Cao Gang Mu): detoxifies, clears the eyes, disperses eye redness and swelling and cloudy films, treats deafness, headache and head soreness, treats phlegm-malaria and harsh breathing, nasal obstruction—when stuffed into the nose the obstruction drops by itself; also disperses sores and swellings.
④ "Essentials of Raw Herbal Natures" (Sheng Cao Yao Xing Bei Yao): treats bruises and fractured bones, relieves pain and reduces swelling.
⑤ "Essentials of Collected Medical Forest" (Yi Lin Zuan Yao): unblocks stagnation, dispels cold, arrests malaria, stops dysentery. A powdered form pinched into the nose can induce sneezing to dispel cold stagnation.
⑥ "Illustrated Examination of Plant Names and Realities" (Zhi Wu Ming Shi Tu Kao): treats sha-syndrome.
⑦ "Guangxi Medicinal Plant Illustrations" (Guangxi Yao Zhi Tu Zhi): treats gan-accumulation (childhood malnutrition).
⑧ "Guangxi Chinese Medicinal Substances" (Guangxi Zhong Yao Wu): treats throat toxin.
⑨ "Guangdong Chinese Materia Medica II" (Guangdong Zhong Yao II): treats whooping cough.
⑩ "Guangzhou Military Common Chinese Herbal Manual" (Guangzhou Bu Dui Chang Yong Zhong Cao Yao Shou Ce): treats rheumatic low back and leg pain.
Usage and Dosage
Internal use: decoct as a decoction, 5–9 g; or mash to extract juice.
External use: appropriate amount, crush and apply as a poultice; or crush and stuff into the nose; or grind to powder and pinch into the nose.
Prescriptions using Small Centipeda Herb (E bu shi cao)
① For wind-cold headache, nasal congestion, eye film: Small Centipeda Herb (fresh or dried both acceptable) rubbed and sniffed to induce sneezing; use twice daily. ("Guiyang Folk Herbal Medicine")
② For cold-phlegm harsh wheezing: juice of Wild-garden-coriander (Ye yuan sui) mixed with wine and taken orally. ("Binhu Ji Simple Formulas")
③ For brain-leak (nasal cerebral leakage): fresh Centipeda (Shi hu sui) crushed and stuffed into the nostrils. ("Zhejiang Folk Herbal Medicine")
④ For single or double throat-swelling (dan shuang hou e): Small Centipeda Herb one liang, glutinous rice (nuo mi) one liang. Crush the herb, take the juice to soak the glutinous rice and grind into a slurry; have the patient slowly hold and swallow. ("Guangxi Commonly Used Folk Herbs")
⑤ For eye disease with swelling and redness, dim vision and light sensitivity, obscure scratching pain, wind itch, nasal obstruction, headache, head soreness, external eye films clinging to the eyeball, thick sticky discharge: Small Centipeda Herb two qian, Indigo naturalis (Qingdai) one qian, Chuanxiong Rhizome (Chuanxiong) one qian. Grind to a fine powder, first hold water in the mouth, then use about a grain-of-rice amount to be pinched into the nose until tears flow; not restricted to time of day. ("Yuan Ji Qi Wei" — Hou Bi Bi Yun San)
⑥ For pterygium encroaching on the eye: fresh Small Centipeda Herb two liang. Crush, extract juice, boil and clarify; add a fragment of borneol (Bingpian) one fen and mix evenly, instill into the eye. ("Guangxi Commonly Used Folk Herbs")
⑦ For spleen-cold malaria: Centipeda (Shi hu sui) a handful, pound to extract half a bowl of juice, add half a bowl of wine and take together. ("Binhu Ji Simple Formulas")
⑧ For quotidian malaria and tertian malaria: fresh Small Centipeda Herb, rub into a ball and insert into the nose; initially it causes sneezing—endure somewhat—after one night it is effective. ("Modern Practical Chinese Medicine")
⑨ For amoebic dysentery: Centipeda (Shi hu sui) and Black-leek root (Wu jiu gen) each five qian. Decoction taken once daily; if bleeding is profuse add Xianhecao (Xian he cao) five qian. ("Jiangxi Herbal Medicine")
⑩ For gan-accumulation diarrhea: fresh Centipeda (Shi hu sui) three qian. Decoction taken orally. ("Hunan Materia Medica")
(11) For acute abdominal pain: inflorescences of Qiuzi cao crushed and smelled through the nose to induce sneezing. ("Zhejiang Folk Herbal Medicine")
(12) For damp-toxin leg ulcers: Wild-garden-coriander (collected in summer and dried to powder) five qian each, mercury powder five fen, mixed with tung oil into a paper-separated plaster, sew around and apply after washing with tea; yellow fluid discharges. ("Simple Single Prescriptions")
(13) For swellings and toxins: Wild-garden-coriander one handful, pangolin scale (charred to retain properties) seven fen, Angelica tail (Danggui wei) three qian. Crush and add one bowl of wine, squeeze and take the liquid, apply the residue as a poultice. ("Binhu Ji Simple Formulas")
(14) For hemorrhoidal swelling and pain: Centipeda (Shi hu sui) crushed and applied as a poultice. ("Binhu Ji Simple Formulas")
(15) For psoriasis: Small Centipeda Herb crushed and applied topically. ("Guiyang Folk Herbal Medicine")
(16) For snakebite: fresh Centipeda (Shi hu sui) crushed and applied externally to the wound. ("Quanzhou Materia Medica")
(17) For traumatic swelling and pain: appropriate amount of Small Centipeda Herb, crushed, stir-fried until hot, and applied to the affected area. ("Guangxi Commonly Used Folk Herbs")
(18) For corn (clavus): first pare down the thickened skin of the corn, then crush fresh Centipeda (Shi hu sui) and pack onto the lesion; remove after three to five days. ("Zhejiang Commonly Used Folk Herbs")

Ba Du San (Ba du san)
Cultivation and processing of Yellow-flowered Sida (Huanghuaren)
Source
The whole herb of the Malvaceae plant Ba Du San (Ba du san). Harvested in autumn, used fresh or sun-dried.
Morphology
Ba Du San is an erect subshrub about 1 m tall. Young branches are covered with stellate long soft hairs. Leaves dimorphic; petiole 5–10 mm long, covered with stellate soft hairs; stipules awl-shaped, shorter than the petiole; lower leaves broadly rhombic to fan-shaped, 2.5–5 cm long, nearly as wide, apex short-acuminate to rounded, base cuneate, margin with two teeth; upper leaves oblong-elliptic to oblong, 2–3 cm long, both ends blunt to rounded, upper surface sparsely covered with stellate hairs or coarse appressed hairs to nearly glabrous, underside densely covered with gray stellate tomentum. Flowers solitary or clustered at branch tips, pedicel about 1 cm long, densely covered with stellate glandular hairs, with nodes above the middle; calyx cup-shaped, about 7 mm long, lobes triangular, sparsely covered with stellate soft hairs; flowers yellow, 1–1.5 cm in diameter, petals obovate, about 8 mm long; stamens about 5 mm long, covered with long stiff hairs. Fruit nearly globose, about 6 mm in diameter, schizocarps of 8–9 mericarps, sparsely covered with stellate soft hairs, with short awns. Seeds dark brown, smooth, 2 mm long, hilum clothed with white soft hairs. Flowering period: June to November.
Habitat and distribution
Ecological environment: grows on barren slopes and in shrubbery, at pine forest edges, along roadsides and stream banks.
Resource distribution: distributed in southwest China and Guangxi and other regions.
Nature and Taste
Bitter; cold
Effects of Yellow-flowered Sida (Huanghuaren)
Functions
The whole herb of the Malvaceae plant Ba Du San (Ba du san). Used for acute mastitis, acute tonsillitis, carbuncles and furuncles, swelling-toxicity, enteritis, bacillary dysentery, amenorrhea in women, and traumatic injuries from falls and blows.
Channels
Lung; Liver meridians
Indications
Clears heat and resolves toxicity, invigorates blood and removes blood stasis. Treats acute mastitis, acute tonsillitis, carbuncles, swelling-toxicity, enteritis, bacillary dysentery, amenorrhea in women, and traumatic injuries.
1. Dian Nan Ben Cao: Treats women's insufficient lactation, mastitis, breast masses, redness and swelling; disperses various sores and swellings with toxin; treats pediatric hematuria and urinary bleeding; relieves skin itching, disperses wind and reduces fever. Stem and leaf powdered finely, mixed with vinegar and applied to carbuncles and ulcerous sores.
2. Yunnan Chinese Herbal Medicine: Invigorates blood and removes stasis, detoxifies, unites bones, and promotes lactation. Treats amenorrhea, carbuncles, gunshot wounds, and fractures.
3. Selected Yunnan Chinese Herbal Medicines: Anti-inflammatory, detoxifying and promotes tissue regeneration. Treats acute mastitis, acute tonsillitis, enteritis, and bacillary dysentery.
Dosage and administration
Internal use: decoction, 9–15 g.
External use: appropriate amount, crush and apply as a poultice.
Precautions and contraindications
Contraindicated in pregnancy.
Formulas of Yellow-flowered Sida (Huanghuaren)
1. For scrofula and carbuncles: crush fresh leaves of Ba Du San (Ba du san) and apply to the affected area. (Selected Yunnan Chinese Herbal Medicines)
2. For traumatic injuries: crush fresh leaves of Ba Du San (Ba du san), add brown sugar or wine, mix and apply to the affected area. (Selected Yunnan Chinese Herbal Medicines)
3. For insufficient lactation: 3–5 qian of Ba Du San (Ba du san), stewed with pig's trotters and taken. (Yunnan Chinese Herbal Medicine)

Source: https://zhongyibaike.com/wiki/%E5%BD%93%E8%8D%AF

Swertiae Herba (Dang Yao)

Bristly Swertia (Liu mao zhang ya cai)
Zhangya Swertia (Zhang ya cai)
Purple-flowered Swertia (Zi hua Dang Yao)
Cultivation and Processing of Swertiae Herba (Dang Yao)
Source
This product is the dried whole herb of the Gentianaceae plant Bristly Swertia SzLertia pseudochinensis Hara. Collected in the summer and autumn seasons, impurities are removed, and it is sun-dried.
Processing
Remove impurities, wash quickly, moisten thoroughly, cut into sections, and dry.
Properties and Meridian Entry
Bitter, cold. Enters the liver, stomach, and large intestine meridians.
Functions and Indications
Clears damp-heat and strengthens the stomach. Used for damp-heat jaundice, hypochondriac pain, dysenteric abdominal pain, and loss of appetite.
Usage and Dosage
Internal use: decoct, 6–12 g, reduce appropriately for children; or grind into powder and take with water.
External use: appropriate amount, crush and apply as a poultice; or apply the expressed juice externally.
Description
This product is 10–40 cm long. Roots conical, 2–7 cm long, yellow or yellow-brown, fracture surface whitish. Stem quadrangular-columnar, often with narrow wings, many-branched, diameter 1–2.5 mm; yellow-green or yellow-brown with purple, nodes slightly swollen; brittle, breaks easily, cross-section hollow. Leaves opposite, sessile; entire leaves when spread flat are strap-shaped-spathulate, 2–4 cm long, 0.3–0.9 cm wide, apex gradually acuminate, base narrow, margin entire. Inflorescences are paniculate-umbellate, terminal or axillary. Calyx deeply 5-lobed, lobes linear. Corolla pale blue-purple or dull yellow, deeply 5-lobed, with two glands at the inner base of each lobe, glands surrounded by long hairs. Capsule elliptic. Slight odor, bitter taste.
Effects of Swertiae Herba (Dang Yao)
Efficacy
This product is the dried whole herb of the Gentianaceae plant Bristly Swertia. Used for damp-heat jaundice, hypochondriac pain, dysenteric abdominal pain, and loss of appetite.
Formulas of Swertiae Herba (Dang Yao)
For acute and chronic bacterial dysentery and abdominal pain: Swertiae Herba 3 qian. Decoction to drink. (The following properties and tastes are from "Inner Mongolia Materia Medica")

Jasmine leaf (Mo Li Ye)
Source: https://zhongyibaike.com/wiki/%E8%8C%89%E8%8E%89%E5%8F%B6
Name
Moli Flower Leaf
Moli Flower Leaf
Cultivation and Processing of Jasmine Leaf
Source
The leaves of Jasmine (Moli), a plant of the Oleaceae family. Harvested in summer and autumn, washed clean, used fresh or sun-dried.
[Original morphology]
Erect or climbing shrub, up to 3 m tall. Branchlets cylindrical or slightly compressed, sometimes hollow, sparsely covered with soft hairs. Leaves opposite, simple; petiole 2–6 mm long, with short soft hairs and a joint. Leaf blade papery, circular, ovate-elliptic or obovate, 4–12.5 cm long, 2–7.5 cm wide, ends rounded or blunt, base sometimes slightly cordate; except for the vein axils beneath which often bear tufts of hairs, otherwise glabrous. Inflorescences cymose, terminal, usually with three flowers, sometimes solitary or up to five; peduncle 1–4.5 cm long, with short soft hairs; bracts minute, conical; pedicel 0.3–2 cm long; flowers very fragrant; calyx glabrous or sparsely with short soft hairs, lobes linear; corolla white, corolla tube 0.7–1.5 cm long, lobes oblong to nearly rounded. Fruit globose, about 1 cm in diameter, purple-black. Flowering May to August, fruiting July to September.
[Habitat and distribution]
Widely cultivated throughout southern China. Originally native to India.
Properties and flavor
Pungent, slightly bitter, warm in nature.
Appearance
Leaves mostly curled and wrinkled; when flattened they are broadly ovate or elliptic, 4–12 cm long and 2–7 cm wide, ends rather blunt, with yellow clustered hairs in the vein axils beneath; petiole short, 2–6 mm long, slightly pubescent. Slight fragrance, slightly astringent taste.
Effects of Jasmine Leaf
Efficacy
The leaves of Jasmine (Moli) of the Oleaceae family. Used for externally contracted febrile disorders, dysentery with abdominal distention, swollen painful feet (beriberi), and poisonous insect stings or bites.
Channels
Lung; Stomach meridians
Indications
Dispel wind and release the exterior; reduce swelling and relieve pain. Indicated for externally contracted fever, dysentery with abdominal distention, swollen painful feet (beriberi), and poisonous insect stings or bites.
Usage and dosage
Internal: decoct, 6–10 g.
External: appropriate amount, decoct for washing or crush and apply as a poultice.

Jiu Ping Hua (Jiu Ping Hua)
Source: https://zhongyibaike.com/wiki/%E9%85%92%E7%93%B6%E8%8A%B1
Names
Little azalea (Xiaodujian), Liangmao azalea (Liangmao dujuan)
Little azalea (Xiaodujian)
Liangmao azalea (Liangmao dujuan)
Cultivation and processing of Azalea (Jiupinghua)
Source
The root of the Ericaceae plant Liangmao azalea (Liangmao dujuan). Collected in summer and autumn. Sliced and sun-dried.
[Morphology]
Evergreen small shrub, 0.5–2 m tall. Branchlets slender and numerous, light brown, densely covered with reddish-brown appressed hairs. Leaves alternate, crowded at branch tips; petiole short, 2–5 mm long, with brown coarse appressed hairs. Leaf blade leathery, oblong, obovate-elliptic or oblong-lanceolate, 1–4.5 cm long, 0.5–2 cm wide, apex acute, shortly acuminate or acuminate, base short cuneate, entire margin, adaxial surface dark green with sparse appressed long hairs, abaxial surface pale green with scattered reddish-brown flattened appressed hairs; midrib slightly prominent on both surfaces, lateral veins and reticulate veins not obvious. Flowers 3–6, borne at branch tips and leaf axils, forming umbel- or raceme-like inflorescences; pedicel 3–6 mm long, with shiny reddish-brown fine hairs; calyx small, 5-lobed or sometimes unlobed, 1–4 mm long, with reddish-brown fine hairs; corolla funnel-shaped, slightly bilaterally symmetrical, light purplish-red, pink, or bright purple, 5-lobed, lobes spreading, the upper three lobes with deep red spots inside; stamens 5, longer than corolla, filaments with fine soft hairs on the lower part, anthers dehiscing by apical pores; pistil 1, ovary 5-loculed, densely covered with reddish-brown long coarse hairs, style slender, glabrous or hairy at the base. Capsule small, ovoid, 4–9 mm long, exterior densely covered with reddish-brown coarse appressed hairs, persistent style, dehiscent into five valves at maturity. Flowering March–May, fruiting June–July.
[Habitat and distribution]
Ecological environment: grows in mountain meadows or hillside scrub at altitudes of 1000–2500 m, under pine forests, in mixed broadleaf forests or under mixed coniferous-broadleaf canopies, frequently found in limestone mountain shrubland.
Resource distribution: distributed in Shaanxi, Sichuan, Guizhou, Yunnan, and other areas.
Properties and flavor
Astringent, cool.
Effects of Azalea (Jiupinghua)
Actions
The root of the Ericaceae plant Liangmao azalea (Liangmao dujuan). Used for common cold, acute and chronic nephritis, pyelonephritis, and pediatric convulsions.
Channels entered
Heart and Bladder meridians
Indications
Clears heat and releases the exterior, promotes diuresis. Used for common cold, acute and chronic nephritis, pyelonephritis, and pediatric convulsions.
Usage and dosage
Oral: decoction, 15–30 g.

Jiu Xian Cao (Jiu Xian Cao)
Source: https://zhongyibaike.com/wiki/%E4%B9%9D%E4%BB%99%E8%8D%89
Cultivation and Processing of Nine-Immortal Herb (Jiu Xian Cao)
Source
It is the whole herb or root of Santalaceae family plants Long-leaved Bairuicao (Changye Bairuicao), Exserted-stigma Bairuicao (Luzhu Bairuicao), Long-flowered Bairuicao (Changhua Bairuicao) or Abrupt-bending Bairuicao (Jizhe Bairuicao). The whole herb is harvested in summer and autumn and sun-dried.
Morphology
Perennial herb, about 50 cm tall. Stems clustered, with obvious longitudinal grooves. Leaves sessile, linear, 4–4.5 cm long, 2.5 mm wide, apex gradually pointed, with 3 veins. Racemose inflorescences axillary or terminal; flowers yellowish-white, bell-shaped, 4–5 mm long; pedicels 0.6–2 cm long; with fine streaks; bract 1, linear, 1 cm long; two bracteoles, narrowly lanceolate, about 4.5 mm long, margins rough; perianth 5-lobed, lobes narrowly lanceolate, apex acute, incurved; stamens 5, inserted at the base of the lobes and enclosed; flowers recessed; ovary stalk 0.5 mm long. Nutlets nearly globose or ovoid, yellow-green, 3.5–4 mm long, surface occasionally with forked longitudinal veins (ribs), persistent perianth shorter than the fruit. Flowering June–July, fruiting August–September.
2. This species differs from Long-leaved Bairuicao (Changye Bairuicao) in that: stems prostrate, branches and leaves sparse; leaves linear, 2.5–3 cm long; flowers nearly bell-shaped; style exserted; nutlets with indistinct longitudinal veins. Persistent perianth inwardly curved and wrinkled. Flowering in June, fruiting in August–September.
3. This species differs from the previous two in that: leaves linear, occasionally linear-lanceolate, 7–17 mm long, with 3 veins; bract located at the base of the pedicel, two bracteoles located beneath the flower, opposite; racemes often compound into panicle-like inflorescences; flowers 6–10 mm long. Nutlets globose, about 4.5 mm wide, surface with longitudinal veins; persistent perianth longer than the fruit. Flowering June–July, fruiting August–September.
4. This species differs from the first three in that: stems with obvious longitudinal grooves. Leaves linear, 3–5 m long, apex often blunt, usually with a single vein. Flowers white; pedicels after flowering incline outward and gradually reflex; one leaf-like bract, two bracteoles; fruit stalk up to 1 cm long, reflexing when fruit is ripe. Flowering in July, fruiting in September.
Habitat and Ecology
1. Grows in grass clumps on barren slopes or under sparse woods.
2. Grows in grass clumps on mountain slopes and under pine forests at altitudes of 2,900–3,700 m.
3. Grows on sunny grassy slopes or under sparse woods at altitudes of 2,600–4,100 m.
4. Grows in meadows or gravelly slopes.
Distribution of Resources
1. Distributed in Northeast China and in Inner Mongolia, Hebei, Gansu, Jiangsu, Sichuan, Yunnan, etc.
2. Distributed in Sichuan and Yunnan.
3. Distributed in Sichuan, Mi Yunnan, Tibet, etc.
4. Distributed from Northeast, North China, Northwest to Southwest regions.
Properties and Flavor
Acrid; slightly bitter; cold in nature
Effects of Nine-Immortal Herb (Jiu Xian Cao)
Efficacy
It is the whole herb or root of Santalaceae family plants Long-leaved Bairuicao (Changye Bairuicao), Exserted-stigma Bairuicao (Luzhu Bairuicao), Long-flowered Bairuicao (Changhua Bairuicao) or Abrupt-bending Bairuicao (Jizhe Bairuicao). Mainly used for treating common cold, heatstroke, pediatric pneumonia, and convulsions.
Channels Entered
Lung; Liver; Spleen channels
Indications
Releases the exterior and clears heat, expels wind and stops spasms. Indicated for common cold, heatstroke, pediatric pneumonia, and convulsions.
Usage and Dosage
Internal use: decoction, 6–12 g; or taken with steamed egg.
Formulas of Nine-Immortal Herb (Jiu Xian Cao)
① For pediatric liver-heat deficiency fever: Jiu Xian Cao (Jiu Xian Cao),
Bupleurum (Chai Hu)
,
Baical skullcap (Huang Qin)
three qian each, decocted in water and taken orally.
② For pediatric malnutrition and night blindness: Jiu Xian Cao (Jiu Xian Cao), ground to powder, cooked with added sugar, or eaten with steamed egg.
③ For gastrocnemius muscle spasms and rheumatic pain: Jiu Xian Cao (Jiu Xian Cao) and Drynaria (Guo Shan Long) each two qian, decocted in water and taken with a dash of wine. (Formula selected from "Kunming Folk Commonly Used Herbs")

Source: https://zhongyibaike.com/wiki/%E8%8B%A6%E4%B8%81%E8%8C%B6
Names
Broadleaf Holly Leaf
Hairy-leaved Huangniu tree (Máoyè Huángniúmù), Yellow pulp fruit (Huángjiāngguǒ), Earth Tea (Tǔchá), Tea Cover (Chágài), Horn-spine Tea (Jiǎocìchá)
Bitter Tea (Kǔchá)
Hairy-leaved Huangniu tree (Máoyè Huángniúmù)
Yellow pulp fruit (Huángjiāngguǒ)
Earth Tea (Tǔchá)
Tea Cover (Chágài)
Horn-spine Tea (Jiǎocìchá)
Cultivation and Processing of Kuding Tea (Kǔdīngchá)
Source
Mainly the leaves of holly family (Aquifoliaceae) plants: Gougu (Gǒugǔ) and Large-leaved Holly (Dàyè Dōngqīng).
Properties and Taste
Sweet; Bitter; Cold
Processing
Remove impurities, shade-dry, set aside.
Characteristics
① Gougu leaves; also called: Horn-spine Tea (Jiǎocìchá) (Gangmu Shiyi). See the Gougu leaf entry for detailed appearance. Leaves from old Gougu trees are also used; leaf blades are ovate-elliptic, apex shortly acute, base rounded, upper surface smooth, coriaceous and thick. Produced in Jiangsu, Zhejiang and other regions.
② Large-leaved Holly leaves; also called: Kudeng Tea (Kǔdēngchá) (Ducao Qiuniu). Leaves are ovate-oblong elliptic, coriaceous, not wrinkled, some longitudinally slightly curled, upper surface yellow-green or gray-green and glossy, underside yellow-green, taste slightly bitter. Produced in Zhejiang, Fujian, Guangxi and other regions.
Effects of Kuding Tea
Therapeutic Effects
Mainly the leaves of holly family (Aquifoliaceae) plants: Gougu (Gǒugǔ) and Large-leaved Holly (Dàyè Dōngqīng).
Main indications: headache, toothache, red eyes, blocked ears, febrile disease with vexation and thirst, dysentery
Meridians
Liver meridian
;
Lung meridian
;
Stomach meridian
Indications
Disperse wind-heat, clear the head and eyes, relieve vexation and thirst. Treats headache, toothache, red eyes, blocked ears, febrile disease with vexation and thirst, dysentery.
① Benjing Fengyuan: stops dysentery.
② Yilin Zuanyao: treats febrile mania.
③ Gangmu Shiyi: expel wind, invigorate blood, induce abortion.
④ Bencao Zaixin: reduce food stagnation and transform phlegm, relieve vexation and stop thirst, promote urination and bowel movements, remove greasiness.
⑤ Bencao Qiuyuan: clear Lung and Spleen, stop dysentery, clear head and eyes.
⑥ Zhongguo Yixue Da Cidian: disperse liver wind, clear head and eyes, treat tinnitus, deafness, blocked ears with purulent discharge, activate blood vessels, cool the uterus.
⑦ Sichuan Materia Medica: can clear heat and disperse wind, relieve vexation and quench thirst. Treats headache, toothache, tinnitus, red eyes, and food stagnation with phlegm.
Usage and Dosage
Internal: decoct, 3–9 g; or include in pill formulations.
External: appropriate amount, decocted water for fumigation and washing, or apply topically.
Precautions and Contraindications
Use with caution in those with spleen and stomach deficiency-cold.
Prescriptions using Kuding Tea
① For treating pulmonary tuberculosis: Gougu tender leaves one liang. Roast dry, steep in boiling water, drink as tea. (Hunan Materia Medica)
② For treating lumbar and joint pain: Gougu leaves soaked in wine and drunk. (Hunan Materia Medica)

Kudzu root (Ge Gen)
Source: https://zhongyibaike.com/wiki/%E8%91%9B%E6%A0%B9
Names
Root of Lobed Kudzuvine,Root of Thomson Kudzuvine,Kudzuvine Root
Dried Kudzu (Gan Ge),Sweet Kudzu (Gan Ge),Fen Ge (Fen Ge),Ge Ma Ru (Ge Ma Ru),Kudzu Seed Root (Ge Zi Gen),Kudzu Strip Root (Ge Tiao Gen),Ji Qi Root (Ji Qi Gen)
Dried Kudzu (Gan Ge)
Sweet Kudzu (Gan Ge)
Fen Ge (Fen Ge)
Ge Ma Ru (Ge Ma Ru)
Kudzu Seed Root (Ge Zi Gen)
Kudzu Strip Root (Ge Tiao Gen)
Ji Qi Root (Ji Qi Gen)
Kudzu (Ge)
Fen Ge Root (Fen Ge Gen)
Roasted Kudzu Root (Wei Ge Gen)
Cultivation and Processing of Kudzu Root (Ge Gen)
Source
This item is the dried root of the Fabaceae plants wild kudzu Pueraria lobata (Willd.) Ohwi or Thomson's kudzu vine Pueraria thomsonii Benth.
Morphology
1. Wild Kudzu (Ye Ge)
A perennial deciduous climbing vine up to 10 m long. The whole plant is covered with yellowish-brown coarse hairs. The tuberous root is cylindrical, fleshy, the outer bark grayish-yellow, inside mealy and very fibrous. The stem base is stout and the upper part is much branched. Leaves are pinnately trifoliate; the terminal leaflet stalk is relatively long; leaf blades rhomboid-ovate, 5.5–19 cm long, 4.5–18 cm wide, apex gradually acute, base rounded, sometimes shallowly lobed, lateral leaflets smaller, obliquely ovate, unequal on both sides, abaxial surface pale with a farinose coating, both surfaces covered with short appressed soft white hairs; stipules are peltate, ovate-lanceolate, small stipules needle-shaped. Racemes are axillary or terminal, corolla bluish-purple or purple; bracts narrow linear, early deciduous, bracteoles ovate or lanceolate; calyx campanulate, 0.8–1 cm long, 5 calyx teeth lanceolate, two upper teeth connate, the lower tooth longer; standard petal nearly round or ovate with a slightly emarginate apex and two short auricles at the base, wings narrowly elliptic and shorter than the standard, often with an auricle at the base on one side, the keel petal slightly longer than the wings; stamens 10, diadelphous; ovary linear, style curved. Legume linear, 6–9 cm long, 7–10 mm wide, densely covered with yellowish-brown long stiff hairs. Seeds ovate, reddish-brown, glossy. Flowering April to August, fruiting August to October.
2. Thomson's Kudzu Vine (Gan Ge Teng)
A vine. Roots enlarged. Stems and branches covered with yellowish-brown short hairs or mixed with long stiff hairs. Leaves trifoliate with long petioles; stipules lanceolate-elliptic with hairs; leaflets rhomboid-ovate to broadly ovate, sometimes 3-lobed, 9–21 cm long, 8–18 cm wide, apex shortly acuminate, base cordate. Racemes axillary; bracteoles ovate; calyx campanulate, 1.2–1.5 cm long, 5 lanceolate calyx teeth longer than the calyx tube, covered with yellow long stiff hairs; corolla purple, 1.3–1.8 cm long. Pods oblong, flattened, 10–12 cm long, 1–1.2 cm wide, densely covered with yellowish-brown long stiff hairs. Seeds reniform or round. Flowering June to September, fruiting August to October.
Taste and Properties
Sweet; Pungent; Neutral
Physical Characteristics
(1) Intact wild kudzu roots are mostly cylindrical. Commercially they are often cut into slanted, longitudinal, or transverse slices of uneven sizes. Surface brown with longitudinal wrinkles, transverse lenticels and irregular rootlet scars visible. Texture firm; fracture rough; yellowish-white in cross-section; 1–3 concentric ring layers faintly visible. Strongly fibrous, slightly farinaceous. Slight aroma, mildly sweet taste.
(2) Fen Ge root is cylindrical, spindle-shaped or semi-cylindrical, some are thick longitudinal or oblique slices of varying sizes. Peel removed, surface yellow-white or pale yellow; unpeeled surface gray-brown. Hard and heavy in texture, less fibrous, in some specimens cottony, very farinaceous. Superior material has large tubers, firm texture, white color, abundant starchiness, and few fibers.
Effects of Kudzu Root (Ge Gen)
Functions
This item is the dried root of the Fabaceae plants wild kudzu or Thomson's kudzu vine.
Main indications: Shanghan and febrile headache with neck stiffness, vexation and fever with excessive thirst, diarrhea, dysentery, rashes that do not surface, hypertension, angina pectoris, deafness.
Channels
Spleen channel; Stomach channel; Lung channel; Bladder channel
Main Uses
Raises yang and releases the exterior, brings out rashes and stops diarrhea, relieves vexation and clears heat. Treats cold damage and febrile diseases with headache and nape stiffness, vexation with fever and thirst, diarrhea, dysentery, rashes that fail to surface, hypertension, angina pectoris, deafness.
1. Ben Jing (The Classic): Treats wasting-and-thirst (Xiao Ke), excessive body heat, vomiting, various obstructions, generates yin qi, and detoxifies poisons.
2. Bie Lu (Alternate Records): Cures cold damage wind-stroke headache, releases the muscles and the exterior, promotes sweating, opens the interstices. Treats traumatic injuries and relieves pain, treats flank wind pain. Fresh root juice treats wasting-and-thirst and severe febrile disease.
3. Ben Cao Jing Ji Zhu (Collected Annotations on Materia Medica): Kills the poisons of wild kudzu, croton, and many poisons.
4. Tao Hongjing: Pounded fresh and the juice drunk to resolve epidemic fever. Kudzu root powdered treats traumatic bleeding and also treats malaria and sores.
5. Yao Xing Lun (Treatise on Medicinal Properties): Treats rebellious qi rising to the head, vomiting, opens the stomach to descend food, antidotes alcohol poisoning, stops vexation and thirst. Boiled powder treats traumatic bleeding and seasonal febrile heat.
6. Tang Ben Cao (Tang Materia Medica): Powder taken orally treats dog bites; drinking the juice is beneficial.
7. Ben Cao Shi Yi (Supplement to Materia Medica): Fresh breaks blood, resolves sores, can induce miscarriage, antidotes alcohol poisoning, treats body heat and jaundice, and painful, scanty urination.
8. Ri Hua Zi Ben Cao (Ri Hua Zi Materia Medica): Treats chest and diaphragm heat, vexation and mania, stops bloody dysentery, unblocks the small intestine, discharges pus and stops bleeding, applied to snake and insect bites.
9. Kai Bao Ben Cao (Kaibao Materia Medica): For children with heat and abdominal fullness, soak and mash kudzu root and give the juice to drink.
10. Yi Xue Qi Yuan (Origins of Medical Learning): Eliminates spleen and stomach deficiency heat and thirst.
11. Zhang Yuan Su: Releases the exterior and dispels evil, promotes eruption of difficult-to-emerge childhood rashes.
12. Compendium of Materia Medica (Ben Cao Gang Mu): Disperses constrained fire.
Dosage and Administration
Internal use: decoction, 10–15 g; or mash and take the juice.
External use: appropriate amount, pound and apply as poultice.
Precautions and Contraindications
1. Zhang Yuan Su: Do not take in large doses for fear of injuring the stomach qi.
2. Ben Cao Zheng (Correct Materia Medica): Its nature is cool and prone to cause nausea; use with caution in those with cold stomach.
3. Ben Cao Cong Xin (New Compilation of Materia Medica): Particularly contraindicated in summer when there is profuse spontaneous sweating due to exterior deficiency.
Prescriptions Using Kudzu Root (Formulas)
1. For Taiyang disease with stiff neck and back, little or no sweat, aversion to wind: Kudzu root 4 liang, Ephedra (Ma Huang) 3 liang (nodes removed), Cinnamon Twig (Gui Zhi) 2 liang (bark removed), Fresh Ginger (Sheng Jiang) 3 liang (sliced), Licorice (Gan Cao) 2 liang (honey-fried), Peony (Bai Shao) 2 liang, Jujube (Da Zao) 12 pieces (quartered). Combine these seven herbs in one dou of water; first boil ephedra and kudzu, reduce by two sheng, remove white scum, add the other herbs, boil to obtain three sheng, strain, warm and take one sheng; this should produce a slight sweat. (From Shang Han Lun: Ge Gen Tang)
2. For Taiyang disease with Gui Zhi pattern where the physician wrongly purged the patient causing persistent diarrhea and a rapid pulse (exterior not yet released), wheezing and sweating: Kudzu root half a jin, Licorice (Gan Cao) 2 liang (honey-fried), Baikal Skullcap (Huang Qin) 3 liang, Coptis (Huang Lian) 3 liang. Use these four herbs in eight sheng of water; first boil kudzu, reduce by two sheng, add the other herbs, boil to obtain two sheng, strain, divide and take warm. (From Shang Han Lun: Ge Gen Huang Qin Huang Lian Tang)
3. For cold-damage epidemic heat with strong fever, wind-heat, headache, limb pain, rashes erupting or not: Cimicifuga (Sheng Ma), Kudzu root (fine grated), Peony (Bai Shao), Licorice (Gan Cao) (grated, honey-fried) in equal parts. Coarsely powder; each dose four qian, water one bowl and a half, decoct to one bowl, take warm as needed. (From Yan's Pediatric Formulas: Sheng Ma Ge Gen Tang)
4. For early-stage measles eruption incomplete with high fever and small papules not yet surfacing: Kudzu root, Cimicifuga (Sheng Ma), Platycodon Root (Jie Geng), Peucedanum root (Qian Hu), Saposhnikovia root (Fang Feng) each one qian, Licorice (Gan Cao) five fen. Decoction to take. (From Quan You Xin Jian)
5. For heat-toxin causing lower bleeding or bleeding triggered by eating hot foods: Fresh kudzu root 2 jin, mash and take one sheng of juice, mix with one sheng of lotus root juice and take together. (From Mei Shi Ji Yan Fang)
6. For incessant vomiting of blood from a heated heart: Fresh kudzu root juice half a da sheng, swallow at once. (From Guang Li Fang)
7. For daily nosebleed not stopping with vexation: Fresh kudzu root, mash and take the juice; each dose one small cup. (From Sheng Hui Fang)
8. For pregnancy heat disease with chest vexation: Kudzu root juice 2 sheng, divided into three doses. (From Shang Han Lei Yao)
9. For sudden persistent retching: Mash kudzu root, wring out the juice, take one sheng less a small amount. (From Bu Que Zhou Hou Fang)
10. For alcohol intoxication not awakening: Kudzu root juice one dou and two sheng, drink and recover consciousness. (From Qian Jin Fang)
11. For food poisoning from vegetables causing madness, vexation, vomiting and diarrhea to near death: Boil kudzu root and give the decoction to drink. (From Bu Que Zhou Hou Fang)
12. For improper dosing of medicine causing bitter vexation in the heart: Drink fresh kudzu root juice generously. If fresh is unavailable, kudzu root powder five he with water may be taken, or it can be decocted. (From Bu Que Zhou Hou Fang)
13. For acute intestinal obstruction: Kudzu root and Gleditsia sinensis (Zao Jiao / Zhu Ya Zao) each 1 jin, add 4000 ml water, boil for 40 minutes, strain; keep the decoction warm on a hot plate at a tolerable temperature. Separately fold ten layers of gauze about one Chinese foot square into four pads, soak in the decoction and wring slightly to remove excess liquid, alternately place on the abdomen as a sustained hot compress, each application one hour, two to three times daily. (Journal of Henan Medical College 9(4):203, 1965)
14. For traumatic injuries with wind-stroke and severe spasms nearing death: Pound one jin fresh kudzu root, cut finely, boil in one dou of water to obtain five sheng, strain and take one sheng warmed; for many, pound to a fine powder, mix three pinchfuls into warm wine. If the mouth is clenched and cannot open, take copious bamboo sap and plenty of fresh kudzu root until spontaneous recovery; diet also beneficial. (From Zhou Hou Fang)
15. For initial cold-damage with headache and internal heat with flooding pulse: Use Kudzu root 4 liang, add two sheng water and one sheng fermented soybean (dou chi), boil together to half a sheng and take. Adding fresh ginger juice is better.
16. For vexation, restlessness, and thirst: Use kudzu powder 4 liang mixed into water in which millet has been soaked overnight, cook and take with rice gruel.
17. For early-stage boils: Burn kudzu vines to ash, mix with water and apply as a poultice.
Dietary Therapy
Kudzu Starch Gruel (Ge Fen Geng)
Kudzu starch 250 g, Schizonepeta spikes (Jing Jie Sui) 30 g, Light fermented soybeans (Dan Dou Chi) 150 g. Make the kudzu starch into noodles; boil Schizonepeta spikes and Dan Dou Chi in water until 6–7 boils, remove dregs and take the liquid, cook the kudzu noodles in the liquid until done. Eat once in the morning and once in the evening.
Efficacy: Nourishes the liver and kidneys, extinguishes wind and opens the orifices. Indications: Suitable for wind-stroke due to liver and kidney yin deficiency, slurred speech, clouded consciousness, hemiplegia, cerebral arteriosclerosis in middle-aged and elderly. Also useful for stroke prevention.

Cultivation and Preparation of Liaogewang (liao ge wang)
Source
Stems and leaves of Nanling Raohua (nan ling rao hua) in the Thymelaeaceae family. Stems and leaves can be harvested year-round; wash, cut into sections, sun-dry or use fresh.
[Original morphology]
Nanling Raohua (nan ling rao hua) is a semi-evergreen small shrub, up to 1 m tall. The whole plant is smooth and hairless. Stems erect, much branched, young branches reddish-brown. Root bark and stem bark are rich in cottony fibers and not easily broken. Leaves opposite, nearly sessile; leaf blades obovate to oblong-elliptic, 2–5 cm long, 0.8–1.5 cm wide, apex obtuse or shortly acuminate, margin entire, base cuneate, many lateral veins very fine, brown when dry. Flowers yellow-green, several flowers clustered at branch tips, arranged in compound umbel-like inflorescences or nearly sessile capitulum-like heads; flowers bisexual, without bracts, perianth tubular, apex 4-cleft, glabrous; stamens 8, in two whorls attached to the inner perianth tube, filaments short, anthers oblong; ovary obovoid or oblong-elliptic, with a rounded stigma. Drupes ovoid or ellipsoid, bright red when mature. Flowering and fruiting in summer and autumn.
[Habitat and distribution]
Ecological environment: grows in hillside shrub thickets, by roadsides and village margins.
Resource distribution: distributed in Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian, Taiwan, Hunan, Guangdong, Guangxi, Guizhou, Yunnan and other areas.
Taste and properties
Taste bitter; pungent; nature cold; toxic
Processing
Steamed leaves can be pounded to a pulp for external application or squeezed for juice and applied externally. Roots can be steamed until cooked, sliced and sun-dried. Steam leaves, wash, air-dry in the shade, cut into sections and set aside.
Characteristics
Stems cylindrical, branched, of varying lengths, 8–25 mm in diameter; surface of thick stems light brown to dark brown-black, with irregular coarse longitudinal wrinkles, lenticels prominent, often two connected transversely, sometimes several connected to form a ring; surface of thin stems dark brown-red, with fine longitudinal wrinkles and opposite leaf petiole scars, sometimes with raised small branch remnants. Hard in texture; fracture surface shows numerous cottony fibers in the cortex. Leaves irregularly curled, when flattened oblong-elliptic, margin entire, pale yellow-green to light green, veins slightly raised beneath; petiole short, about 2 mm long. Brittle, easily broken. Odor faint, taste slightly bitter.
Therapeutic effects of Liaogewang (liao ge wang)
Functions
Stems and leaves of Nanling Raohua (nan ling rao hua) in the Thymelaeaceae family. Indicated for suppurative swellings and sores; scrofula; rheumatic pain; traumatic injuries from falls and blows; snake and insect bites.
Meridians
Heart; Lung; Small Intestine channels
Indications
Clears heat and detoxifies, transforms phlegm and disperses nodules, reduces swelling and relieves pain. Mainly used for suppurative swellings and sores, scrofula, rheumatic pain, traumatic injuries, snake and insect bites.
Usage and dosage
Internal: decoction (should be decocted for a long time, more than 4 hours), 6–9 g;
External: appropriate amount, pounded and applied, powdered and mixed for topical application, or decocted for washing.
Precautions and contraindications
Avoid in individuals with weak constitutions and in pregnant women.
Formulas using Liaogewang (liao ge wang)
① For phlegm-fire sores (nodular ulcers in the axilla or groin or cramping pain of the limbs): Liaogewang leaves 5 qian, add a little table salt, pound together and apply to the affected area. (Lingnan Materia Medica)
② For "hexi feng" (crane-knee wind): Nanling Raohua (nan ling rao hua), Jiegucao (jie gu cao). Decoction with water, take with wine. (Hunan Materia Medica)
③ For sores and toxic swellings; traumatic injuries from falls and blows; snake and insect bites; infant scalp sores: fresh Liaogewang stems and leaves, pounded and applied externally or squeezed for juice and applied externally. (Guangzhou Military Handbook of Common Chinese Herbs)
④ For sores and breast abscesses: an appropriate amount of Liaogewang leaves, pounded and applied to the lesion. (Guangxi Materia Medica)
⑤ For unnamed swellings and toxins: Dinggewang leaves (ding ge wang), pounded, add a small amount of rice wine, apply to the affected area. (Jiangxi Herbal Handbook)
